UGraduate App Vignette

Spring 2026, DATA-413/613: Final Project

Author

Adaobi (Myles) Nwatu, Evan Blizzard, Natalie Cope

1 Use Case

Selecting peer institutions for benchmarking and identifying which institutional characteristics are associated with student retention are two of the most common analytical tasks in institutional research. Both are typically done with small, hand selected comparison sets. Our app, UGraduate addresses this somewhat arbitrary means of identifying peers and analyzing retention by giving users a data-driven alternative using the IPEDS dataset of U.S. postsecondary institutions.

The app supports four core tasks: tracking institutional metrics over time, exploring bivariate relationships between institutional characteristics, identifying structurally similar peers via Euclidean distance across user-selected variables, and fitting a multivariate linear model of retention to compare an institution’s actual retention against what its admissions, pricing, financial aid, and program profile would predict.

The app is designed for institutional researchers, university administrators, and particularly curious prospective students and families.

2 App Details

2.1 Packages and Versions

This app was built using the packages in Table 1. {renv} was used to manage and lock dependencies.

2.2 Data Source and Structure

Data Source. The app uses publicly available federal data from the Integrated Postsecondary Education Data System (IPEDS), administered by the National Center for Education Statistics (NCES) within the U.S. Department of Education (U.S. Department of Education, National Center for Education Statistics 2024). IPEDS collects institution-level data annually from every Title IV-eligible postsecondary institution in the U.S., covering enrollment, admissions, completions, retention, financial aid, tuition and fees, and institutional finances. Because Title IV participation is basically a universal precondition for federal student aid, IPEDS is essentially a census of U.S. higher education (rather than a sample) which makes it the appropriate foundation for an institutional benchmarking tool.

Ingestion. IPEDS distributes annual data as Microsoft Access database files, one per academic year, downloaded directly from the NCES IPEDS Data Center. Each annual database contains dozens of tables corresponding to different IPEDS surveys (admissions, enrollment, finance, etc.). During preprocessing, the relevant tables from each year were extracted, variables of interest were pulled from each, some variables were created from existing ones, and the per-year frames were merged into a single long-format data frame, master_data, with one row per institution per academic year. This dataframe is saved as data/master_data.RData and loaded once at app startup.

Structure. master_data covers 2019-20 through 2023024, with 14,408 rows and 14 columns. There is one row per institution-year, across 3,105 unique institutions. Variables include identifiers (unitid, instnm, city, stabbr, control, academic_year), retention and demographic outcomes (ret_pres, pell_pct) and cost, selectivity and program structure measures (applicants, admissions, admit_rate, net_price_avg, net_price_avg_pell, hhi_score).

Restrictions on use. IPEDS is U.S. federal government data and is in the public domain, so there are no licensing fees, redistribution restrictions, or registration requirements for accessing or using the data. NCES requests that users cite IPEDS as the source in any publications or public-facing materials, per standard NCES citation guidance. Because the data are institution-level aggregates rather than student-level records, there are no FERPA or individual privacy restrictions on use.

3 Exploratory Data Analysis Workflows

3.1 Exploratory Data Analysis I: Institutional Trends

Scenario. An institutional research analyst at American University wants to understand how AU’s first-year retention rate has shifted over the past several years, and whether nearby nonprofit peers in DC have experienced similar trends. Before running any models or distance calculations, they want to look at the data by plotting one variable at a time across years to identify the pattern.

Workflow: The app’s global sidebar drives every tab. They select Private Nonprofit under Select Sector, which dynamically populates the Select State(s) dropdown with only the states that have nonprofit institutions in the filtered data. They pick DC, then uses the searchable Select Peer Institution(s) box to add American University, Georgetown, and George Washington University. This three-step filter (sector to state to school) prevents impossible combinations. They cannot, for example, ask for a public school in a state that has none in the dataset.

From the global sidebar they look over at the Institutional Trends tab. Its local sidebar offers one control: a radio-button Select Metric list with seven choices (retention rate, Pell %, HHI specialization, two net-price variants, admission rate, and total admissions). They select Retention Rate. The main panel renders an interactive Plotly line chart with one line per selected school, colored by institution, across academic years on the x-axis. See Figure 1.

Interpreting the output. The analyst reads three things off the chart. First, level. Georgetown sits consistently above AU and GWU, reflecting its more selective admissions profile. Second, trajectory. All three schools show a decline going into 2020-21, then an increase in 2021-22, followed by a decline to around pre-pandemic levels for the remaining academic years. Third, volatility. The COVID-era cohort shows up immediately with sharp decreases in retention following the onset of the pandemic in the spring semester of the 2019-2020 academic year. She then switches the metric to Pell % to check whether the same schools’ Pell-eligible student share moved in tandem with retention, which would suggest the two metrics co-vary. See Figure 2.

Responsible Data Science Considerations. Three things matter:

  1. Missing Data filtering: The app drops any institution missing values on the core set of benchmarking variables (ret_pres, pell_pct, hhi_score, net_price_avg, net_price_avg_pell, admit_rate, admissions) before anything is plotted. This keeps every tab consistent, but it also means schools with incomplete IPEDS reporting are invisible in the trend view. The analyst should not interpret a DC comparison set as “all DC nonprofits.”
  2. Autoscaling: Plotly auto-scales the y-axis to the selected schools, so a three-point range can look as dramatic as a thirty-point range. Differences should always be read against the axis, not the steepness of the line.
  3. Single-metric framing: A line chart can show that a metric fell or rose, but not why. The analyst should use the Trends tab to generate hypotheses, not for confirmation.

3.2 Exploratory Data Analysis II: Explore Relationships

Scenario. After examining how retention changes over time, the analyst now wants to understand how retention relates to other institutional characteristics. Specifically, they are interested in whether variables such as program specialization (HHI), admissions rate, or financial aid composition are associated with higher or lower retention across institutions.

Workflow. The analyst keeps the same global sidebar selections used in the Institutional Trends tab (sector, state, and selected institutions). They then navigate to the Explore Relationships tab. In this tab, they select variables for the x- and y-axes (e.g., HHI Score vs. Retention Rate). The app dynamically filters the dataset based on the sidebar inputs and renders an interactive Plotly scatterplot. If enabled, a regression line is added to show the overall relationship between the selected variables. Selected institutions are highlighted, while all other institutions appear in the background for context. See Figure 3.

Interpreting the output. The analyst reads three things from the plot. First, direction. An upward-sloping pattern suggests a positive association between the variables, while a downward slope suggests the opposite. Second, strength. If the points cluster tightly around the regression line, the relationship is more consistent; if they are widely dispersed, the relationship is weaker. Third, outliers. Institutions that fall far from the general pattern may indicate unusual characteristics or data quality issues. The highlighted schools allow the analyst to evaluate how their selected institutions compare to the broader national distribution.

Responsible Data Science Considerations.

  1. Correlation vs. causation: The scatterplot shows associations, not causal relationships. A visible trend does not imply that one variable causes changes in another.
  2. Missing data: Institutions missing values for either selected variable are excluded from the plot, which may affect the observed relationship.
  3. Overplotting: With a large dataset (~4000 schools), points may overlap, making patterns harder to interpret. Transparency and highlighting help mitigate this.
  4. Model simplification: The regression line provides a simplified summary of the relationship and may not capture nonlinear patterns or interactions between variables.

4 Statistical Analysis Workflows

4.1 Statistical Analysis I: Peer Benchmarking

Scenario. The same institutional research analyst has now looked at AU’s retention trend over time (EDA I) and how retention relates to other variables across DC-area nonprofits (EDA II). Their next question is: which institutions nationally are most similar to AU on the dimensions she cares about, regardless of geography? A DC-only list of peers is convenient but technically arbitrary. It may exclude institutions more similar to AU that could be better comparisons on admissions selectivity, pricing, and program mix. They want a data-driven list of peers.

Workflow. They reduce their school selection to just AU. They then move to the global sidebar’s Peer matching variables multi-select picker, which offers the same seven metrics used elsewhere in the app. They select four: Admit Rate, Avg Net Price, Pell %, and HHI Score, which is their definition of what makes institutions comparable. They click Find My Peers.

They then open the Peer Benchmarking Tab. Its local sidebar has one control (Academic Year) which they set to 2023-24. The main panel renders a sortable DataTable showing AU’s ten closest peers nationally, ranked by Euclidean Distance. See Figure 4.

How the distance calculation works. The app uses standard z-score normalization before computing distances. Every selected variable is centered at zero and scaled to unit standard deviation across the full pool for the chosen year. This matters because the variables are on wildly different scales: admit rate runs 0-100, net price runs into the tens of thousands of dollars, HHI is bounded 0-1. Without normalization, net price would dominate the distance calculation and the other three variables would be effectively invisible. After scaling, each variable contributes equally to the distance, and the returned distance is unitless. A distance of 0.5 means “close”; a distance of 3 means “far.” The numbers are only meaningful relative to each other because they are unitless.

The user can also select multiple schools at once. If they put AU, Georgetown, and GWU in the sidebar selector, the table returns ten peers for each, with the Your School column identifying which school each peer row corresponds to.

Interpreting the output. The analyst reads the peer list three ways. The first is face validity: do these schools make intuitive sense? If AU’s top peers include, say, Boston University and GWU they already considered comparable, the matching variables they chose are doing reasonable work. Second is surprises: any unexpected peer is worth investigating because it either reveals a genuine similarity they had not considered, or it means they should reconsider their variable selection. Thirdly, distance gaps: if the top peer has distance 0.4 and the tenth has distance 2.1, AU has a tight comparison set. If distances are all clustered around 1.5, AU is unusual on this variable combination and no institution is a clean match.

Responsible Data Science Considerations.

  1. The peer set is a user-construct. It is entirely dependent on the user selected variables. The analyst should report the variable set alongside any peer list.
  2. Euclidean distance treats all variables as independent and equally weighted, which is rarely true. For example, admit rate and net price are correlated, so matching on both partially double counts selectivity. A correlation-aware distance would be more defensible, but we used Euclidean as a reasonable attempt within the time frame.
  3. Missing data exclusion: the function drops any school missing a value on any of the selected matching variables before computing distances, so a school that looks like a great peer on three variables but is missing a fourth never appears in the list.
  4. Distances aren’t probabilities. “AU’s nearest peer has distance 0.4” is not a statement about how likely the relationship is; it’s just a sorted ranking.

4.2 Statistical Analysis II: Retention Modeling

Scenario. Peer benchmarking tells the analyst which schools are similar to AU, but not what predicts retention within the peer pool. Their next question is: holding admissions selectivity, net price, Pell share, and academic specialization constant, which of these factors is associated with higher retention, and by how much? They want a fitted model with interpretable coefficients, a view of AU’s predicted vs actual retention, and enough diagnostics to determine whether the model is valid.

Workflow. They keep their sidebar set as before: AU selected as the main school. They open the Retention Modeling tab, whose local sidebar has one control: Academic Year, set to 2023-24. The tab contains two sub-tabs: Results and Model Diagnostics.

The Results sub-tab fits an OLS regression of retention rate on admit rate, average net price, Pell percentage, and HHI score across all institutions in the pool with complete data for the chosen year. It renders two outputs stacked: a coefficient plot with 95% confidence intervals, and a predicted-vs-actual scatter. See Figure 5.

Interpreting the coefficient plot. The analyst reads of the direction, magnitude, and precision of each predictor. A negative coefficient on admit rate would mean that more selective schools (lower admit rate) have higher retention, holding everything else constant. A positive coefficient on net price would mean higher-priced schools retain better controlling for everything else, which could be plausible if price is interpreted as a proxy for resources per student. The width of the confidence interval matters as much as the point estimate: a predictor whose CI crosses zero is not distinguishable from no effect in this sample, and the plot colors it accordingly.

The card below the coefficient plot displays the model’s \(R^2\) and adjusted \(R^2\), phrased in plain language (“the model explains X% of the variation in retention rates”). This helps with interpretation: if \(R^2\) is 0.25, four predictors explain a quarter of the variation across institutions and the remaining three-quarters is driven by factors the model does not include.

Interpreting predicted vs actual. The scatter places AU in context. If AU’s point sits on the 45-degree line, its retention rate is exactly what the model predicts given its inputs (AU is neither over nor underperforming on retention relative to other institutions). If AU sits meaningfully above the line, it retains students better than its admissions, price, Pell, and HHI profile predicts. Below the line is the reverse. The colored vs gray layering lets the analyst see AU’s retention and its position in the residual distribution at the same time.

The Diagnostics sub-tab. The analyst clicks over to Model Diagnostics, which renders a residuals-vs-fitted plot and a normal Q-Q plot side by side. These check the assumptions behind the coefficient plot’s confident intervals. See Figure 6

Responsible data science considerations.

  1. The model is not causal. It describes which institutional characteristics are correlated with retention in a given year, not what would happen if a school changed one of them. For example, “Lowering admit rate would raise retention” is not a claim the model supports.
  2. Four predictors is a small model. Retention is driven by innumerable factors. A very high \(R^2\) would actually be suspicious in a model with this few predictors.
  3. The comparison pool is all schools nationally. This means the model is assuming the retention generating process is similar at, say, a 40,000 student research university and a 900 student liberal arts college. This could be rectified if the model was stratified by enrollment size or some other controlling variable, but it is not in our implementation.
  4. Missing data exclusion. Any school missing any of the four predictors is dropped entirely, which can bias the sample toward better-reporting institutions.

5 LITERATURE REVIEW REPRISE

UGraduate combines five important area of studies together: federal post-secondary data, unexplored factors that contribute to student retention, understanding the effects that economics play into program specialization and data-driven peer benchmarking to create an interactive, user-friendly research tool.

Each of the analytical modules in the app is grounded in established research practices and the design choices reflect real discussion within the conversation on higher education. Including variable section, normalization strategy, modeling approaches, and responsible-use warnings reflect real considerations from scholars and university administrative bodies.

This sections reviews this literature, and connects it back to the various strategies used in the app’s implementation of the previously stated considerations

  1. ETHICAL CONSIDERATIONS:
    1. IPEDS Data Infrastructure
      1. IPEDS is designed to help NCES meet its mandate to report full and complete statistics on the condition of post-secondary education in the United States, collecting institution-level data in areas including enrollment, admissions, graduate rates and other outcome measures, retention rates, student financial aid, tuition and fees, faculty staff, and finances.
      2. This mandatory reporting structure is what makes IPEDS the right foundation for a tool targeting institutional comparisons: the data-set is not a convenience sample. The span of coverage means that geographic and sector filters in UGraduate’s global sidebar draw on a near-complete census of U.S. post-secondary institutions rather than a selective sample.
      3. For researchers and institutional administrators using UGraduate, one responsible-use implication flows directly from IPEDS’s design. IPEDS data are used at the federal and state level for policy analysis and development and at the institutional level for benchmarking and peer analysis.
        1. However, the data-set’s unit of analysis is the institution, not not the student. Additionally, IPEDS reports aggregate rates, not individual records, meaning that the OLS model in the UGraduate Retention Modeling tab is an ecological regression, and its coefficients should not be interpreted as individual-level causal effects. This has been noted in the app’s disclaimer.
    2. Missing Data & Sample Bias
      1. IPEDS reporting completeness varies across institutions and variables. Institutions with incomplete records on any of the core benchmarking variables are excluded from analysis. This approach is consistent with standard practice in institutional benchmarking, where incomplete reporters are excluded to ensure comparability, but it introduces the risk that the analysis disproportionately reflects better-resourced institutions with more complete reporting capacity.
    3. Pell Grant Equity Data Transparency
      1. The Retention Gap tab is the most equity-focused component of UGraduate, directly comparing overall institutional retention against the retention rate for Pell Grant recipients. The gap between these two rates is a meaningful signal of whether an instition serves its lowest-income students as well as its broader population.
      2. The Pell Grant itself has a well-documented relationship with student persistence. A $1,00 increase in Pell boosted retention by 1.5% according to a 2011 study in Social Science Quarterly that used data from the nationally representative Beginning Postsecondary Study. Yet despite the program’s direct retention effect, aggregate outcome gaps between Pell and Non-Pell students remain large. An analysis of data from 1,149 public and nonprofit institutions that award bachelor’s degrees found 14% national gap between the completion rates for Pell students (51%) and Non-Pell students (65%).
        1. Institutional-level gaps are smaller on average but highly variable, roughly 35% of institutions have completion gaps if 3% of less, while others exhibit dramatically larger disparities.
        2. These patterns have equity implications that extend beyond individual institutions. Only 28% of Pell Grant recipients attend the most competitive institutions, while 73% attend the least competitive ones; a disparity that has major implications for social mobility and equity in higher education. This distributional fact interacts with UGraduate’s sectors filter: users comparing retention gaps across public and private nonprofit institutions are implicitly comparing populations with different Pell concentration, different levels of institutional resources, and different structural incentives to close the gap.
          1. Most recently, research on “equity engines” which are institutions that both enroll and graduate high proportions of Pell students, highlights how rare strong performance on both dimensions is. When it comes to colleges where Pell Grant recipients are at least 55% likely to graduate, nearly half states don’t have them at all.
          2. Retention Gap tab gives institutional researchers a direct view into this dimension without requiring access to specialized equity-audit platforms.
    4. Program Specialization (The HHI Score)
      1. UGraduate uses a HHI score to quantify each institution’s degree of academic program specialization. The HHIO is a well-established concentration measure from industrial economics. The is calculated by squaring the market share of each competing firm in the industry and then summing the resulting numbers. When applied to higher education, “the market shares” become the proportions of degrees conferred in each CIP program area. A high HHI score indicates an institution highly concentrated in small number of program areas ( a specialist school), while a low HHI score indicates a broad distributional spread (a generalist university).
      2. The application of HHI beyond its antitrust origins to characterize concentration within a single entity across multiple domains has precedent in organizational research. HHI captures whether attention is concentrated in few domains (specialist) or distributed across many (generalist), providing a single score.
        1. In the context of higher education institutions, specialist profile (high HHI) is typically associated with professional schools, technical colleges, and institutions with focused missions, environments where students may benefit from strong co-curricular resources tailored to a single field.
        2. A generalist profiles (low HHI) is associated with comprehensive universities offering a wide range of programs. The relationship between specialization and retention is theoretically ambiguous, specialist environments may generate strong student belonging and focused career pathways while generalist environments provide academic flexibility which is precisely why the app tests it empirically as regression predictor rather than assuming a direction.
  2. TECHNICAL CONSIDERATIONS:
    1. Using Regression to Model Student Retention
    2. R-Shiny as a Platform for Institutional Research
      1. UGraduate is built in R Shiny, a framework specifically designed to turn statistical analyses into interactive web applications with requiring end users to have any programming expertise. Dashboards combining IPEDS data with other federal sources in R Shiny allow higher education administrators, institutional researchers and postsecondary policymakers to select institutions, learn their costs and enrollments, check their historic enrollment and compare them to others, investigate demographic and outcomes data, and make comparisons between institutions. The existence of peer applications in the literature validates this design choice and establishes that the IPEDS + R Shiny combination is a respected choice when creating institutional research tooling.
      2. The broader case for interactive visualization in research comes down to two factors: usability and cognitive access. The available of online scientific journals and articles has creative new opportunities for dynamic, interactive, data visualization which adds cognitive benefits and supports the ability to understand data more fully.
        1. In UGraduate’s case, our target users need to be able to explore many variable combination and comparisons quickly. The Plotly-based charts throughout the app allow hover-based inspection of individual data points, a feature that static reports cannot replicate and that is particularly valuable in the predicted-vs-actual scatter in the Retention Modeling tab.
    3. Visualization Framing Effects
      1. Plotly’s auto-scaling behavior in the Institutional Trends tab can make small institutional differences appear visually dramatic. This is documented challenge in data visualization for policy audiences: axis scaling choices shape perceived magnitude of effects in ways that are independent of statistical significance. The app’s responsible-use note directly calls out this ricks, instructing users to read differences against the axis labels rather than the visual steepness of trend lines.

6 CONCLUSION

UGraduate began with a simple observation: the two most common tasks in institutional research—choosing peer institutions and understanding what predicts student retention—are routinely performed in ways that are more arbitrary than they need to be. Peer groups are often assembled by hand, based on geography, athletic conference membership, or reputational familiarity. Retention analyses are often confined to internal dashboards that compare a single institution to itself over time. Both approaches leave available data on the table.

The app addresses this by giving institutional researchers and administrators a self-service environment for data-driven peer selection and retention analysis, built entirely on a federal data source that is freely available, annually updated, and covers every Title IV-eligible institution in the country. The five analytical modules—Institutional Trends, Explore Relationships, Peer Benchmarking, Retention Gap, and Retention Modeling—are designed to be used in sequence. A user begins by orienting themselves to their institution’s longitudinal profile, moves through bivariate relationship exploration, identifies nationally comparable peers using their own definition of similarity, examines equity gaps for their lowest-income students, and finally situates their institution within a regression model that benchmarks actual retention against what the institution’s structural profile would predict.

Each of these steps involves deliberate design choices that trade interpretive power against simplicity. Euclidean distance with z-score normalization is transparent and reproducible, but does not account for correlations between matching variables. OLS regression is interpretable and assumption-checkable through the diagnostics sub-tab, but operates on institution-level aggregates, cannot support causal claims, and omits many factors—campus culture, advising infrastructure, student demographics not captured in IPEDS—that are known to influence retention. The four-predictor model is deliberately small; a high R² in such a model would be a warning sign, not a success criterion. These are not failures of the implementation; they are properties of the chosen methods, and the app’s responsible-use language names them directly.

The equity orientation built into UGraduate reflects a conviction that retention data are only partially useful if they mask disparities between the institution’s overall performance and its performance for its most financially vulnerable students. The Retention Gap tab makes this disparity legible at the institutional level, and the Pell percentage predictor in the regression model allows users to examine whether the financial aid profile of an institution’s student body is associated with aggregate retention outcomes across the sector. The literature reviewed in the preceding section documents a persistent 14-percentage-point national gap between Pell and non-Pell completion rates—a gap that institutions can either replicate or challenge. UGraduate surfaces the data that lets researchers see which side of that divide their institution falls on.

Taken together, UGraduate demonstrates that a small, carefully scoped Shiny appgitlication built on publicly available federal data can support the kind of exploratory and comparative analysis that institutional research offices often lack the tooling or time to conduct from scratch. Future development could extend the app in several directions: stratifying the regression model by sector or enrollment size to reduce the assumption that a 900-student liberal arts college and a 40,000-student research university share the same retention-generating process; incorporating Mahalanobis distance in the peer benchmarking module to account for correlations between matching variables; adding graduation rate outcomes alongside first-year retention to support longer-horizon analysis; and expanding the equity gap visualization to disaggregate by race and ethnicity as IPEDS reporting of those breakdowns improves. Each of these extensions would make the tool more analytically defensible while preserving the design principle that motivated it
